title: Grip and Vehicle Dynamics
intro: A car can only brake, turn and accelerate as hard as its tyres let it. This page explains where grip comes from, why a tyre has to slip a little to work, how the forces of braking and cornering share one budget, how weight moving around the car changes that budget at each corner, and how wings add grip at speed. These ideas are the base of every other page in this topic.

blocks.text: Tyres and friction

Each tyre touches the road over a contact patch roughly the size of a hand. Every force on the car, except gravity and the air, passes through those four patches. The most force a tyre can make is roughly its friction coefficient $\mu$ times the load pressing it down, $F_{max} \approx \mu F_z$. A typical road tyre on dry tarmac has $\mu$ around 0.9 to 1.0; a warm racing slick, a soft tyre with no tread, reaches 1.4 to 1.7. Wet roads, cold tyres, dust and worn rubber all lower it.

Without wings, the whole car can therefore turn, brake or accelerate at about $\mu$ times gravity. A road car on good tyres corners at about 0.9 to 1 g; a GT race car on slicks at about 1.4 to 1.6 g before downforce; a modern high-downforce single-seater well over 4 g in fast corners, almost all of it from the wings and floor.
Slip: a tyre has to slide a little to grip

Rubber grips by deforming: the tread in the contact patch is stretched and twisted against the road, and it is that distortion that makes the force. So a tyre making a sideways force always points in a slightly different direction from the one it is travelling in. The angle between the two is the slip angle. Under braking or acceleration, the tyre likewise turns slightly slower or faster than the road passes under it; the difference as a fraction of the road speed is the slip ratio.

Force rises steeply with slip at first, peaks, and then falls away slowly as more and more of the contact patch slides. The peak is where the fastest driving happens: a racing tyre typically peaks at a slip angle of roughly 4 to 10 degrees and a slip ratio of roughly 10 to 15 percent. Past the peak the car is sliding, the tyre overheats and wears, and the force drops. Anti-lock brakes and traction control are machines for holding the slip ratio near the peak.

The plot uses the Pacejka "magic formula", $F = D \sin\left(C \arctan(B \alpha)\right)$, the standard empirical fit to measured tyre curves, with $D$ the peak force and $\alpha$ the slip angle. The three curves are the same tyre at half, one and one and a half times the chosen load. Note that 50 percent more load gives less than 50 percent more peak force. That is load sensitivity, and it matters below.

A tyre that is slightly past its peak gives a warning: the steering goes light, the tyre squeals more, the car stops responding to more steering. A tyre with a sharp drop after the peak (high shape factor) gives less warning and is harder to drive at the limit.
The friction circle: one grip budget

A tyre's grip is shared between directions. If it is using all of its grip to brake, it has none left to turn; if it is turning at the limit, any braking or throttle pushes it past the limit. Plotting the car's acceleration with braking and accelerating on one axis and cornering on the other gives the friction circle (in practice an ellipse, sometimes called the traction circle or g-g diagram). A fast driver keeps the car on the edge of it as long as possible, blending from braking into cornering and from cornering into accelerating instead of doing one thing at a time.

blocks.alt: A circle with accelerating at the top, braking at the bottom and left and right turning at the sides. A red trace runs from the centre straight down to the bottom edge (braking), around the edge to the right side (turning while the brakes are released), then up the edge towards the top right (accelerating out of the corner).
blocks.caption: The trace a skilled driver makes through one right-hand corner stays on the edge of the circle. A novice's trace makes an L shape: brake, release, then turn, with time spent inside the circle where grip is wasted.

blocks.text: Weight transfer

When a car brakes, its centre of mass, which sits above the road, tries to keep going, so load moves off the rear tyres and onto the fronts. Accelerating does the opposite, and cornering moves load from the inside tyres to the outside ones. The total weight does not change, only where it sits. For braking or accelerating at $a$ (in m/s²), a car of mass $m$ with its centre of mass at height $h$ and a wheelbase $L$ moves this much load between the axles:

blocks.caption: Longitudinal load transfer. For cornering, replace the wheelbase $L$ with the track width $t$ to get the transfer from the inside to the outside tyres.

widget.title: Axle loads under braking and acceleration

blocks.text: Weight transfer matters because of load sensitivity. Put one tyre on an axle with more load and the other with less, and the loaded tyre gains less grip than the unloaded one loses, so the axle as a whole has less grip than before. That is why a low centre of mass and wide track help, why the end of the car with more load transfer tends to slide first, and why setup changes such as stiffer anti-roll bars (which move more of the cornering load transfer to that end of the car) change a car's balance. It is also why a driver can use the brakes to load the front tyres and help the car turn in.
Balance: understeer and oversteer

A car's balance is which end reaches its grip limit first. If the front tyres slide first, the car turns less than the steering asks and runs wide: understeer, also called push or tight. If the rear slides first, the back steps out and the car turns more than asked: oversteer, also called loose. A neutral car uses both ends near their limit together. Most race cars are set up slightly understeering at the limit because understeer is easier to control, though a fast driver often wants a car that rotates freely on entry.

blocks.alt: Two panels. Left: a car whose front wheels are turned hard runs on a wider path than the dashed line the driver wants. Right: a car whose rear is sliding outwards points into the corner more than the dashed line, and the driver counter-steers.
blocks.caption: Understeer runs wide nose first; oversteer swings the tail out. Both mean one axle has used up its grip.

items: Power-on oversteer: too much throttle in a low gear makes the driven rear tyres spin, so they lose cornering grip. Fixed by easing the throttle gently.
Lift-off (trailing-throttle) oversteer: lifting off the throttle mid-corner moves load forward, unloading the rear tyres, and the tail swings out. Common in front-engined and front-wheel-drive cars.
Entry understeer: turning in while still braking too hard, so the front tyres have no grip left for steering. Fixed by braking a little earlier or releasing the brake more smoothly.
Mid-corner and exit understeer: asking for more speed than the front tyres can hold. On exit, adding throttle in a front-wheel-drive car can make it worse because the fronts must also drive.

blocks.text: Tyre temperature, pressure and wear

Tyres grip best in a temperature window, often around 80 to 100 °C for racing slicks. Cold tyres slide; overheated tyres lose grip and wear fast. This is why drivers weave and brake hard on an out lap and why the first lap after a pit stop is slow. Pressure rises as the tyre heats, and the working (hot) pressure is what counts. Too high a pressure shrinks the contact patch and makes the tyre skittish; too low lets the sidewall roll and overheats the shoulders. Over a stint the tyre wears and loses grip (degradation), which drives race strategy. Graining (small rolls of rubber torn from a tyre that slides while too cold) and blistering (rubber overheating from within) are two common failure patterns.
Aerodynamics: downforce and drag

Wings and a shaped floor push the car down onto the road without adding mass, so the tyres gain grip without the car becoming harder to accelerate. Both the downforce and the drag grow with the square of speed:

blocks.tex: F_{down} = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho\, v^2 C_L A, \qquad F_{drag} = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho\, v^2 C_D A
blocks.caption: $\rho$ is the air density (about 1.2 kg/m³), $A$ a reference area and $C_L$, $C_D$ the lift and drag coefficients.

blocks.text: Downforce therefore helps a lot in fast corners and hardly at all in slow ones. Without it, the fastest steady speed round a corner of radius $r$ is $v = \sqrt{\mu g r}$: doubling the radius only raises the speed by about 41 percent. With downforce, the grip grows as the speed does, so fast corners can be taken far faster than this. More wing means more drag, so it costs speed on the straights; choosing the trade-off for each track is a central setup decision (see #/racing/car-setup). A car following close behind another loses some of its downforce in the disturbed (dirty) air, which is why high-downforce cars struggle to follow through fast corners, while the reduced drag in the same wake helps them on the straights (the slipstream, see #/racing/racecraft).

widget.title: How fast can a corner be taken?

blocks.text: The plot solves $m v^2 / r = \mu \left(m g + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 C_L A\right)$ for $v$, capped at the car's top speed. Lighter cars gain more from the same downforce, because the same push is a bigger share of their weight.

blocks.title: Cornering speed
blocks.text: A car on tyres with $\mu = 1.2$ and no downforce takes a corner of radius 50 m. What is the fastest steady speed? How much faster could it go round a 200 m corner?
blocks.hint: Use $v = \sqrt{\mu g r}$ with $g = 9.81$ m/s², then convert m/s to km/h by multiplying by 3.6.
solution: Four times the radius gives twice the speed: about 48.5 m/s, or 175 km/h. Speed grows only with the square root of the radius.
blocks.answer: about 87 km/h at 50 m and 175 km/h at 200 m

blocks.title: Load transfer under braking
blocks.text: A 1,200 kg car with its centre of mass 0.45 m above the road and a 2.6 m wheelbase brakes at 1.2 g. How much load moves from the rear axle to the front?
blocks.hint: Use $\Delta F_z = m a h / L$ with $a = 1.2 \times 9.81$ m/s².
solution: That is about 2.4 kN, roughly a fifth of the car's 11.8 kN weight, taken off the rear tyres and added to the fronts. It is why the rear brakes must do less work than the fronts (see brake bias on #/racing/car-setup).
